Facilitating Breaking the Shell

Allow at least an hour, or up to two hours if the group needs time to talk. Bring a change people are already trying to make, sticky notes, pens, and four sheets of paper. You can also record the discussion in the browser exercise.

Running the session

  1. Agree the change (5 minutes). Ask someone to describe what would be different for a colleague or a person using the service. Check that the group recognises it.
  2. Collect the barriers (15 minutes). Give people two minutes to write their own sticky notes, one obstacle per note. Read them out and add the ones that occur to people as they listen. Stack duplicates. Keep notes separate if they mean different things.
  3. Pause (10 minutes). Leave the list on display while people take a break.
  4. Introduce the four cards (5 minutes). Read the descriptions together. Ask who would have to act for each kind of barrier to move.
  5. Sort the notes (10 minutes). Give everyone a chance to move a note and explain why. If people disagree about a rule, record how they’ll check it.
  6. Agree actions (15 minutes). Read the notes back. What can someone test? Who else needs to be involved? Put a name and a date beside each action.

The four categories

Brick walls

Outside the group’s authority

The group has checked the constraint and can’t remove it in the time available. A statutory deadline is one example.

Which part is fixed? What can we still change about how we meet it?

Paper walls

An assumption one person can check

Someone says that a manager must approve every referral. Ask to see the rule or find a recent referral where another person made the decision.

Who could check this before the group meets again?

Partition walls

A change that needs somebody else’s help

Two teams want to share a rota. Changing it might take a budget decision, a change to a contract, or time from the people who draw it up.

Who has the authority, information, or time we need?

Mindset issues

A belief that people have come to share

If everyone expects a complaint to lead to blame, staff may learn to keep quiet. Inviting one person to speak up leaves the rest of the arrangement in place.

What happens here that keeps the belief alive? What could we try together?
